statute.text:
1. Remove a post that presents a false safety claim as established or official fact.
2. Allow opinion, personal experience, and disputed advice, even when it is wrong.
3. Escalate to a human moderator when real harm is plausible but the record cannot settle whether rule 1 applies.

case.author: greenthumb_42
case.text: Stop buying weed killer! Mix 1 gallon vinegar, 1 cup salt and a squirt of dish soap. It's 100% safe for vegetable beds — the EPA even recommends it as the organic option.

guidance.judge: Remove only on a clear violation; when unsure, escalate.

filing.reason: I concede: the post presents its recipe as “100% safe” for vegetable beds and as an EPA-recommended organic weed killer, not merely as personal experience or disputed advice. The record indicates those are materially misleading safety/official-endorsement claims: salt can damage soil and migrate to nearby plants ([s5]), and the extension guidance specifically warns against using this mixture near plants and trees one wants to protect ([s4]). EPA-registered acetic-acid herbicides carry significant handling warnings, and EPA registration is not an endorsement of this homemade mixture ([s6]). Rule 2 protects opinions, experiences, and disputed advice, but these categorical assertions leave no reasonable basis to advocate allowing the post under this statute.

filing.claim: Escalate for human review. The post presents a categorical safety assurance and attributes the recommendation to the EPA, while the thread and available guidance raise a plausible risk of lasting soil and collateral damage. That warrants prompt review, but the record does not directly establish whether the exact mixture and the meaning of “100% safe” meet rule 1: the cited guidance discusses risks from salt and vinegar generally, and the EPA material retrieved does not address this recipe or confirm the claimed recommendation. The author’s patio-crack anecdote does not resolve safety in vegetable beds.

The idea of using Dawn soap or any liquid dishwashing soap is to act as a surfactant which means a sticky substance that can hold water against a surface (the vinegar against the plant tissue). [...] There is herbicidal vinegar on the market with a concertation of 20% that is effective against broadleaf weeds. But it can be toxic to handle. Our everyday kitchen vinegar is at a concentration of 5%. So pretty diluted compared to the true herbicidal vinegar.

The University of Maryland Extension has an in-depth article, Vinegar: An Alternative to Glyphosate? This was shared in a previous Ask Extension question. [...] So if you have young weeds with only 1-2 leaves in walkways or driveways I would say go for it and use the vinegar, dish soap and salt to kill the weeds. But if they are near plants and trees you care about, please don't use these agents.

Instead, consider pulling them out by hand and mulching the area for weed suppression.

I hope that I answered your question. Don't hesitate to ask additional questions.

Sincerely,

Most herbicides break down in the soil quicker than salt, which can remain at plant-toxic levels for years if overdone.

Rubbing alcohol and borax are two other DIY ingredients that are slow to break down in the soil and relatively weak in weed-killing ability.
